sample.unit_of_observation: person-year (worker x event time relative to the accident year)
selection_rules: Work accidents that caused a loss to workers' earning capacities (AES assessment)
Work accidents with a physical impact on workers; psychological shocks excluded
Workers with stable employment before the injury, defined as full-time employment in the three years leading up to the accident
Main analysis focuses on workers whose initial education provides direct access to higher degrees
Section IIIB focuses on craft workers, about 70 percent of injured workers with access to higher education
Section IV (marginal treatment effects) restricts to injured workers below age 50 at injury

Non-injured comparison workers satisfy the pre-event employment requirements and do not experience a work accident in the event year; the 'Match' control is drawn one-to-one within cells of age, gender, education level, occupation and industry
sample.n_observations: 14,481 injured workers and 14,481 matched controls (Table 1); 4,568 'Access' and 2,844 'No access' workers (Table 2)

construction_notes: Human capital investment is measured in full-time equivalents (Figure 1 note).
Labor earnings are measured in percent of workers' average earnings in year -1 (Figures 5 and 7 notes).
Physical ability is the average importance of static strength, explosive strength, dynamic strength, trunk strength and stamina, as measured by O*NET (Table 3 note).

Cognitive ability is the average importance of fluency of ideas, originality, problem sensitivity, deductive reasoning, inductive reasoning, information ordering, category flexibility, mathematical reasoning and number facility, as measured by O*NET (Table 3 note).

Occupational Earnings Premium is the average labor market earnings within each 'Match' (Year-Occupation-Industry-Education-Age-Gender) cell in the full population of non-injured workers with at least three years full-time work leading up to year -1 (Table 3 note).

Table 3 columns 1 and 2 are measured in standard deviations from the average occupational earnings premium of the 'No injury' workers matched on calendar year; column 3 reports the percent change in the worker's outcome.
Inverse probability weights come from a logistic regression of access to higher degrees on the covariates reported in Table 2 (Supplemental Appendix D.2).
Reskilling is defined as pursuing a higher degree within 10 years after the accident (Figure 6 note).

Physical jobs are occupations with physical requirements greater than 0.5 standard deviations above the mean; manual jobs follow Autor, Levy, and Murnane (2003) with the same 0.5 standard deviation rule (Figure 7 and Table 5 notes).
Table 4 present discounted values are computed for an injured worker of age 32, the average among the instrument compliers; effects at years 9-10 after injury are extrapolated until retirement age.
Long-term displacement follows the official Danish definition: receiving public transfers for at least 52 total weeks in the first 2 years upon displacement (Table 5 note).

In Table 5, a degree is considered to give access to less physical (manual) jobs if its target occupation is at least 1 standard deviation lower in physical (manual) requirements than the worker's initial occupation; only vocational bachelor's and academy profession degrees count as stackable higher degrees.
Disability benefits are set at 19,000 kroner ($2,700) per month; State Education Support is 6,400 kroner ($900) per month.

Table 3 defines the treatment variable as D x E, where E equals 1 if the worker has completed his degree and is employed 10 years after the accident, because job characteristics are measured for employed workers only.
